parameterNotes.service: the service whose pool opened against the wrong endpoint; both write shares are its writes, so the name is the subject of both.
parameterNotes.configMap: the ConfigMap the rollout renamed a key in; the readings are where the rows landed, and a ConfigMap name is not a quantity any series could hold.
parameterNotes.declaredKey: the key the new deployment declares; the case's point is that it is not the key the application reads, which is a name rather than a number.
parameterNotes.staleKey: the key left behind that still holds the staging URL, and the one the application reads first; naming it is the mechanism, and no reading is per key.
parameterNotes.declaredValuePointsAt: the endpoint the declared key names; the evidence is the share of writes that landed at the other one, so this is the contrast rather than a reading.
parameterNotes.staleValuePointsAt: the endpoint the stale key names, which is where every write went; the staging share states that as a quantity, and the name says which endpoint it is.

groundTruth.rootCauseReason: The rollout renamed the ConfigMap key that carries the primary JDBC URL. The old key was left in place and still holds the staging URL, and the application reads the old key first, so every instance opened its pool against staging. Nothing failed because nothing was asked to fail: the staging database accepts the same schema and the same statements, so every write returned success. The defect is in which endpoint the configuration resolved to, and the only trace of it is the destination of the writes.

rootCauseIndicators.description: every order write lands in the staging database, from the first instance after the rollout
the production database receives nothing, which is the reading the business noticed first and the application never reported
the write error ratio stays at zero throughout, which is what makes this a configuration fault rather than an availability one

causalChain.mechanism: the application resolves its primary JDBC URL by reading the old ConfigMap key first, that key survived the rename holding the staging value, and every instance came up with its pool pointed at staging -- which accepts the same schema, so every write succeeded

evidenceCheckpoints.description: all of the traffic, not most of it: a share of one is what a single resolved endpoint produces, and what a partial rollout or a retry storm cannot
the production database receives nothing after the rollout, which is the direct evidence for a destination rather than a rate
no write failed, which rules out the pool, the credentials and the network -- every explanation that would have produced an error

remediation.action: delete the stale key rather than leaving it beside the renamed one, so a reader cannot resolve a value the rollout meant to replace
refuse to start when the resolved primary URL does not name the production endpoint, so a silent misdirection becomes a failed deploy

sli.none: this case carries the share of writes that reached staging, the share that reached production and the share that failed, and a share of writes is not a duration whichever of the three the fault moved.

query: Orders stopped arriving in the production database, yet every write reported success and no alert fired. Which component is the root cause, and why did nothing fail?
